starter_episodes.title: Why do Irish people never cut this tree?
starter_episodes.hook: Why do Irish stories say you should never cut a lone hawthorn?
starter_episodes.context: In Irish folklore, certain lone hawthorns are treated as fairy property.

beats.beat_1: People believed fairies gathered under these trees. Cutting one could anger them.
beats.beat_2: Even today, roads have been re-routed around lone hawthorns in Ireland.
beats.beat_3: People tie ribbons to them, leave offerings, and walk around them with respect.

starter_episodes.meaning: It's really a story about respect: for nature, for old things, and for land that isn't just ours.
starter_episodes.prompt: Have you ever seen a tree people wouldn't cut? Tell me.

starter_episodes.title: The real meaning of Samhain
starter_episodes.hook: What if Halloween started as something completely different?
starter_episodes.context: Samhain was the ancient Irish festival marking the end of harvest.

beats.beat_1: It fell on the night between October 31st and November 1st. Summer ended. Winter began.
beats.beat_2: People believed the boundary between worlds grew thin. Ancestors could visit.
beats.beat_3: Families lit bonfires, left food out, and welcomed the spirits of loved ones home.

starter_episodes.meaning: It wasn't about fear. It was about remembering: the harvest, the year, and the people who came before.
starter_episodes.prompt: Do you have a tradition for remembering loved ones? Share it.

starter_episodes.title: What happens if you take a selkie's coat?
starter_episodes.hook: What if someone could become a seal just by wearing a coat?
starter_episodes.context: In Irish and Scottish coastal stories, selkies were seal-people.

beats.beat_1: They lived as seals in the sea, but could shed their skin and walk on land as humans.
beats.beat_2: If someone found and hid their sealskin, the selkie couldn't return to the water.
beats.beat_3: In the stories, selkies often lived on land for years, but always longed for the sea.

starter_episodes.meaning: It's a story about belonging. About the pull of home. And about what we lose when we hold too tightly.
starter_episodes.prompt: Where do you feel most at home? Ocean or land?

starter_episodes.title: Why do Irish people leave ribbons at wells?
starter_episodes.hook: Why are there thousands of wells in Ireland covered in ribbons and tokens?
starter_episodes.context: Holy wells have been sacred in Ireland for over a thousand years.

beats.beat_1: People visited them for healing, blessing, and to mark important moments in life.
beats.beat_2: They would walk around the well a certain number of times, say prayers, then leave something behind.
beats.beat_3: Ribbons, coins, and small objects are tied to nearby trees as offerings.

starter_episodes.meaning: It's not just superstition. It's a way of marking a moment, making a wish visible, and connecting to the past.
starter_episodes.prompt: Have you ever visited a wishing well? What did you wish for?

starter_episodes.title: What is a púca and why is it so tricky?
starter_episodes.hook: What if there was a creature that could become any animal it wanted?
starter_episodes.context: The púca is one of Ireland's most famous shapeshifters.

beats.beat_1: It could appear as a horse, a goat, a rabbit, or even a dark-haired human.
beats.beat_2: Púcas were known for mischief: leading travelers astray, but rarely causing real harm.
beats.beat_3: After Samhain, wild blackberries were considered 'púca-spat' and left alone.

starter_episodes.meaning: The púca reminds us that not everything wild is dangerous. Some mischief is just nature having fun.
starter_episodes.prompt: If you could shapeshift into one animal, what would it be?

starter_episodes.title: The real meaning of Bealtaine
starter_episodes.hook: What did Irish people do on the first day of summer, three thousand years ago?
starter_episodes.context: Bealtaine marked the beginning of the bright half of the Celtic year.

beats.beat_1: It fell on May 1st. Winter was gone. Cattle went out to summer pastures.
beats.beat_2: People lit great bonfires on hilltops. They drove cattle between two fires for protection.
beats.beat_3: May flowers decorated doorways. Yellow flowers especially, like primrose and buttercup.

starter_episodes.meaning: Bealtaine was about hope and beginnings. Light returning. The promise that warmth would last.
starter_episodes.prompt: What's your favourite sign that summer is coming?

starter_episodes.title: The legend of Fionn and the Salmon of Knowledge
starter_episodes.hook: What if all the world's wisdom was trapped inside a single fish?
starter_episodes.context: In Irish legend, Fionn mac Cumhaill was destined to eat the Salmon of Knowledge.

beats.beat_1: The salmon had eaten hazelnuts from a sacred well and gained all wisdom.
beats.beat_2: A poet named Finnegas caught it after seven years of trying. He gave Fionn the job of cooking it.
beats.beat_3: Fionn burned his thumb on the fish, sucked it, and accidentally gained the knowledge himself.

starter_episodes.meaning: Sometimes the greatest things come to us by accident. Wisdom finds those who are ready, even unexpectedly.
starter_episodes.prompt: When did you learn something important completely by accident?

starter_episodes.title: Why do Irish people make Brigid's crosses?
starter_episodes.hook: Why do thousands of Irish homes have the same woven cross above their door?
starter_episodes.context: On February 1st, Irish people make crosses from rushes for St Brigid's Day.

beats.beat_1: Brigid was both an ancient goddess and a beloved saint. Her day marks spring's beginning.
beats.beat_2: The cross is woven from fresh rushes gathered that day. Each family makes their own.
beats.beat_3: Once hung above the door, it's said to protect the home from fire and harm for the year.

starter_episodes.meaning: Making something by hand, together, to protect your home. That's what tradition really means.
starter_episodes.prompt: Does your family have any handmade traditions? Tell me about them.

starter_episodes.title: How the Giant's Causeway was really made
starter_episodes.hook: What if a giant built a road across the sea just to fight another giant?
starter_episodes.context: The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland has 40,000 hexagonal stone columns.

beats.beat_1: Legend says the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to walk to Scotland and challenge a rival.
beats.beat_2: When the Scottish giant turned out to be huge, Fionn's wife disguised him as a baby.
beats.beat_3: The Scottish giant fled, terrified of how big the 'father' must be. He tore up the causeway behind him.

starter_episodes.meaning: Sometimes the cleverest solution isn't fighting at all. It's making your enemy think twice.
starter_episodes.prompt: Have you ever solved a problem by being clever instead of strong?

starter_episodes.title: What is Wren Day and why do people dress up?
starter_episodes.hook: Why do people in Ireland dress in straw and hunt for wrens on December 26th?
starter_episodes.context: St Stephen's Day, December 26th, is also known as Wren Day in Ireland.

beats.beat_1: Traditionally, boys would hunt a wren, carry it door to door, and ask for money or treats.
beats.beat_2: Today, people dress in straw suits and colourful costumes, parading through towns with music.
beats.beat_3: The wren is now fake or just represented. It's become a celebration of community and tradition.

starter_episodes.meaning: Old traditions change. What matters isn't the original meaning, but the community that keeps it alive.
starter_episodes.prompt: Does your town have any unusual local traditions? I'd love to hear about them.
